subject: No validator checks that instruction text names a command the box actually implements
description:
Nancy, 2026-09-14, answering whether a CLASS fix exists for the defect that recurred three times today. It does not. Checked: box-hint-help-level-lint.js (BOX-010) audits hint specificity vs declared tier -- a different axis. box-walkthrough-audit.js (BOX-002a) checks a walkthrough EXISTS and explicitly states it does not check content. Nothing under _tools/eduscan/box-*.js asks 'does this error/notify/hint string name a token that resolves to a real command in this box's dispatch table'. THE DEFECT IT WOULD CATCH: pr001's spooler failure printed 'Clear C:\Windows\System32\spool\PRINTERS\'. The operator typed 'clear ...', got "'clear' is not recognized ... Did you mean: cls" -- cls clears the SCREEN. Four sites in one file carried that same instruction; I fixed one, Nancy found the other three, and two of them (the Services Start/Restart buttons) are the path the box's OWN hints recommend. SHAPE OF THE FIX, same as SHELL-004 and BOX-003's allowlist: extract candidate command tokens from student-facing strings (notify(), returned terminal output, hint text, ticket bodies), resolve each against the box's commands object plus the Terminal.js builtin surface, and flag any imperative that names a token the box cannot answer. Must be baseline-gated -- there will be pre-existing hits -- and must not fire on prose that merely contains a verb ('Clear the paper path' is a physical action, not a command). The walkthrough-verbatim harness CANNOT cover this: it replays only commands printed at a prompt in the walkthrough, so an undocumented-but-recommended path like a GUI button is structurally invisible to it.
[2026-09-15 00:38] SCOPE CORRECTION from Nancy, 2026-09-14: this is NOT mechanical like BOX-003's allowlist. BOX-003 resolves engine.<name> against a derived member set -- a lookup. This requires distinguishing an IMPERATIVE naming a command ('Clear C:\Windows\System32\spool\PRINTERS\') from ordinary prose describing a physical action ('Clear the paper path', 'Replace the separation pad'). That is a classification problem, and nobody has measured what the false-positive rate would be against ~1800-line box configs full of narrative ticket text, hint prose and simulated tool output. BEFORE building: sample the corpus and measure. If the rate is high, the narrower and still-valuable rule is to check only strings that already contain a filesystem path or a token matching a known command name, rather than every imperative verb. A gate that cries wolf on teaching prose gets bypassed, and a bypassed gate is worse than none.
